Louis XIV :: Health and death :: Succession :: chunk_0039
Louis outlived most of his immediate legitimate family. His last surviving legitimate son, [Louis, Dauphin of France](/wiki/Louis,_Grand_Dauphin "Louis, Grand Dauphin"), died in 1711 of smallpox and barely a year later, [Louis, Duke of Burgundy](/wiki/Louis,_Duke_of_Burgundy "Louis, Duke of Burgundy"), the eldest of the Dauphin's three sons and then heir-apparent to Louis, died of measles. Burgundy's elder son, [Louis, Duke of Brittany](/wiki/Louis,_Dauphin_of_France_(1707%E2%80%931712) "Louis, Dauphin of France (1707–1712)"), died of the same disease a few weeks later. Thus, on his deathbed, Louis's heir-apparent was his five-year-old great-grandson, [Louis, Duke of Anjou](/wiki/Louis_XV "Louis XV"), Burgundy's younger son.

Louis foresaw that his successor would not yet be mature and sought to restrict the power of his nephew [Philippe II, Duke of Orléans](/wiki/Philippe_II,_Duke_of_Orl%C3%A9ans "Philippe II, Duke of Orléans"), who, as his closest surviving legitimate relative in France, would probably become [regent](/wiki/Regent "Regent") to the prospective Louis XV. Accordingly, the king created a regency council as Louis XIII had in anticipation of Louis XIV's own minority, with some power vested in his illegitimate son [Louis-Auguste de Bourbon, Duke of Maine](/wiki/Louis-Auguste_de_Bourbon,_Duke_of_Maine "Louis-Auguste de Bourbon, Duke of Maine").[[129]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDunlop2000454–455-131) Orléans, however, had Louis's will annulled by the Parlement of Paris after his death and made himself sole regent. He stripped Maine and his brother, [Louis-Alexandre, Count of Toulouse](/wiki/Louis-Alexandre_de_Bourbon,_comte_de_Toulouse "Louis-Alexandre de Bourbon, comte de Toulouse"), of the rank of [Prince of the Blood](/wiki/Prince_du_Sang "Prince du Sang") that Louis had granted them and significantly reduced Maine's power and privileges.[[130]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAntoine198933–37-132)

Flag of Wyoming :: Symbolism :: chunk_0003
The symbolism of the Wyoming state seal as detailed in the statute reflects both the state's history and values: the eagle and shield represent the United States and Wyoming's position as the 44th state; the central female figure embodies the political position and rights of women, with broken chains signifying freedom and progress; the male figures symbolize the key industries of livestock and mining; the two pillars and lamps signify the light of knowledge; the scrolls identify the primary economic sectors; and the dates "1869–1890" mark the organization of the Wyoming Territory and the state's admission to the Union.[[2]](#cite_note-WY83101-2)

In 1919, the Wyoming state legislature appropriated funds to print and distribute pamphlets for schoolchildren, containing color-embossed copies of the state flag along with explanatory remarks about its design. The pamphlet explained that the seal on the bison represents the western custom of branding, and that the bison itself was once "monarch of the plains." The red border symbolizes both the Native Americans, who "knew and loved our country long before any of us were here," and the blood of pioneers who gave their lives reclaiming the land. White signifies purity and uprightness, while blue, reminiscent of Wyoming's skies and distant mountains, represents fidelity, justice, and virility. Finally, the pamphlet notes that the red, white, and blue of Wyoming's flag correspond to the colors of the Stars and Stripes of the United States, the "greatest flag in all the world."[[3]](#cite_note-3)

Methionine :: A proteinogenic amino acid :: Encoding :: chunk_0003
Methionine is one of only two amino acids encoded by a single [codon](/wiki/Codon "Codon") (AUG) in the standard [genetic code](/wiki/Genetic_code "Genetic code") ([tryptophan](/wiki/Tryptophan "Tryptophan"), encoded by UGG, is the other). In reflection to the evolutionary origin of its codon, the other AUN codons encode [isoleucine](/wiki/Isoleucine "Isoleucine"), which is also a hydrophobic amino acid. In the mitochondrial genome of several organisms, including [metazoa](/wiki/Vertebrate_mitochondrial_code "Vertebrate mitochondrial code") and [yeast](/wiki/The_yeast_mitochondrial_code "The yeast mitochondrial code"), the codon AUA also encodes for methionine. In the standard genetic code AUA codes for isoleucine and the respective tRNA (*ileX* in *Escherichia coli*) uses the unusual base [lysidine](/wiki/Lysidine_(nucleoside) "Lysidine (nucleoside)") (bacteria) or [agmatidine](/wiki/Agmatidine "Agmatidine") (archaea) to discriminate against AUG.[[13]](#cite_note-13)[[14]](#cite_note-14)

The methionine codon AUG is also the most common start codon. A "Start" codon is message for a [ribosome](/wiki/Ribosome "Ribosome") that signals the initiation of protein [translation](/wiki/Translation_(biology) "Translation (biology)") from mRNA when the AUG codon is in a [Kozak consensus sequence](/wiki/Kozak_consensus_sequence "Kozak consensus sequence"). As a consequence, methionine is often incorporated into the *N*-terminal position of [proteins](/wiki/Protein "Protein") in [eukaryotes](/wiki/Eukaryote "Eukaryote") and [archaea](/wiki/Archaea "Archaea") during translation, although it can be removed by [post-translational modification](/wiki/Post-translational_modification "Post-translational modification"). In [bacteria](/wiki/Bacteria "Bacteria"), the derivative [*N*-formylmethionine](/wiki/N-Formylmethionine "N-Formylmethionine") is used as the initial amino acid.
